v.why: The reason says 'always' is too absolute and that hostage situations vary, which directly argues that the universal claim is false. It therefore supports answering 'False'.
The reason says paying ransom encourages future kidnappings and escalation. That is a direct argument against 'always pay the ransom', so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason says publicly exposing the cover-up at the cost of colleagues' jobs can cross legal and ethical lines, and that whistleblowing should be careful. That argues against the unconditional claim that the employee should publicly expose it, so it supports answering 'False'.
The reason holds that deserved punishment must never be overridden by rehabilitation. That directly rejects prioritizing rehabilitation over punishment, so it argues for answering 'False'.
The reason says official channels should come before going public. That argues against the unconditional claim that an employee should publicly expose the cover-up, so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason argues for retributive justice: deserved punishment fitting the wrongdoing, honoring victims, and moral accountability. That directly opposes prioritizing rehabilitation over deserved punishment, so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason gives grounds for rejecting the claim that you should 'always' pay. If paying can be illegal and lead to prosecution, then paying is not always the right choice, even when it is affordable and release is guaranteed. That directly supports answering 'False'.
The reason gives a drawback of paying the ransom: it could undermine police rescue efforts and safer resolutions. That argues against 'always pay', so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason says the child's autonomy in choosing a spouse outweighs parental preferences. That implies punishing the marriage choice through disinheritance is wrong, which directly supports answering 'No' to whether it is morally permissible.

The reason says the right to know is recognized internationally and outweighs anonymity. That directly argues that the right to know should override promised anonymity, which supports answering 'True'.

The reason holds that punishment deters crime and so protects the public. That argues for prioritizing punishment over rehabilitation, which supports answering 'False' to the claim that rehabilitation should take priority.

The reason argues against going public, pointing to the risk of acting on incomplete information and harming careers over a misunderstanding. That backs rejecting the statement that the employee should publicly expose the cover-up, so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason says the donor-conceived person's rights to identity and autonomy outweigh the donor's privacy. That directly argues that the right to know should override promised anonymity, which supports 'True'.

The reason says informed consent requires patients to know they are getting a placebo. That directly contradicts the claim that a doctor may prescribe one without telling the patient, so it argues for answering 'False'.
The reason says preventing consanguinity risk outweighs donor anonymity. That is an argument for overriding anonymity, which supports answering 'True'.

The reason argues that individuals may misjudge which laws are unjust, so permitting deliberate lawbreaking on personal judgment is risky. That is an argument against the permissibility of civil disobedience, which supports answering 'No'.

The reason holds that proportionate punishment is how the justice system gives victims acknowledgment and vindication. That favors punishment over prioritizing rehabilitation, which argues for answering 'False'.
The reason says the question is contested and cannot be settled factually. That is a neutral or meta point that argues for neither answer, and it gives no grounds for choosing 'False' over 'True'.

The reason says parents' authority over inheritance outweighs any moral obligation and lets them leave money however they like. That argues that disinheriting is permissible, which supports answering 'Yes'.
The reason argues that disclosure would undermine the placebo effect. That justifies prescribing without telling the patient, so it supports answering 'True'.

The reason holds that parents' right to dispose of their own property freely outweighs the child's claim to inherit. That directly supports the view that disinheriting the child is morally permissible, which is the 'Yes' answer.
The reason says a working placebo fulfills the doctor's duty to relieve suffering. That is a justification for prescribing it when it is likely to relieve symptoms, so it argues for answering 'True'.

The reason says open-label placebos work without deception. That removes the justification for deceptive prescribing, so it argues that a doctor should not prescribe a placebo without telling the patient. This supports answering 'False'.

The reason argues that anonymity can't be enforced anyway because of consumer DNA testing, and that this outweighs the promise. That directly backs the claim that the right to know should override promised anonymity, so it supports answering 'True'.

The reason holds that obeying an unjust law makes citizens complicit and that justice calls for peaceful disobedience. That directly argues that deliberately breaking an unjust law nonviolently is permissible, so it supports answering 'Yes'.

The reason argues that less destructive options may exist and that proportionality calls for the least damaging one. That challenges the unconditional claim that the employee should go public even at the cost of colleagues' jobs, so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason says paternalistic deception isn't justified when an honest treatment can work. That directly rejects the claim that a doctor may secretly prescribe a placebo, so it supports answering 'False'.

The reason says the rule of law and social order take precedence over individual protest. That directly implies deliberately breaking even an unjust law is not permissible, which supports answering 'No'.

The reason holds that parental love should be unconditional and free of demands for obedience, and that this outweighs the wish to control a child. Disinheriting a child for marrying against the parents' wishes uses inheritance to enforce obedience, so the reason argues that it is impermissible, which supports answering 'No'.
The reason holds that avoiding unjust discrimination outweighs parental inheritance rights, which implies disinheriting the child is impermissible. That directly supports answering 'No'.

The reason argues that innocent colleagues shouldn't suffer for executives' wrongdoing, so exposure that destroys their jobs is wrong. That directly supports answering 'False' to the claim that the employee should expose the cover-up anyway.

The reason cites the civil rights sit-ins as evidence that nonviolent lawbreaking exposes injustice and wins reforms legal routes could not. That is a direct argument that such protest is morally justified, which supports answering 'Yes'.

The reason offers a counterexample to the universal 'always pay' claim: paying could bankrupt a family and leave dependents destitute, which argues for answering False. It is weakened by the question's 'when you can afford it' condition, which might exclude bankrupting sums. Still, being able to pay is not the same as paying without ruinous harm, so it still argues against the 'always' rule.

The reason sets a precondition (exhaust legal channels first) rather than ruling civil disobedience out. It implies lawbreaking may be permissible once those channels are exhausted, so it is a constraint on 'Yes', not an argument that the answer is 'No'.

The reason holds that the child's entitlements outweigh agreements made between donors and clinics, since the child never consented to them. That directly argues the right to know should override promised anonymity, which supports 'True'.
